Walk through your first review
  1. Open the example or your source. Keep the original file alongside your saved work.
  2. Make it readable. Open Reading & image tools. Expand Adjust the view for image zoom, brightness, contrast, and background; expand Adjust reading size and spacing for text comfort.
  3. Compare one passage. Keep the original OCR. Edit Your proposed reading only where the source supports it; describe uncertainty.
  4. Choose how to read it (optional). Under Reading context, choose a starter example or your own context. Its exact version is saved with your reading.
  5. Explain and save. Add your name, passage location, and what you checked. Save the proposed reading.
  6. Invite a second check. Under Decisions & history, a reviewer or mentor records their reasoning. Disagreements stay visible.
  7. Take your work with you. Use Save as… for a review record, readable text, or PDF. Reopen the review record to replay saved steps.

Interpretation check: preserve the estimate’s qualifications

No OCR defect is asserted in this passage. The task is to distinguish a theoretical estimate under stated production assumptions from a measured result. Keeping the wording unchanged can be the correct outcome.

  1. On page 61, find “maximum theoretical daily atmospheric losses.” Preserve the qualifying words.
  2. On page 51, compare the design-capacity scenario with the lower-production scenario. Record which assumptions belong to each estimate.
  3. Follow the footnotes. Mark the underlying 1971 memo as not independently inspected unless you acquire and inspect it.
  4. The starter context “Estimates and their assumptions” is selected under Reading context. Read its meaning; a mentor can record a check of that exact version under Contexts.
  5. Explain your check in Reason for this reading, add your name, and save. A mentor can then record a second check under Decisions & history.

No correction is required when the wording is already accurate. A useful contribution may be a documented check or an unresolved question.

Real-source exercise: read the Anniston expert report, page 61, then compare page 51. Which assumptions qualify the estimate? Record those qualifications rather than treating an estimate as a measurement. This exercise does not establish court admissibility or a historical discovery by Reckoner.

READING CONTEXTS

Say how a passage should be read

A context, which some people call a lens, is a named and versioned statement of meaning: what its terms mean, the rules it applies, and what a reader should check. Choose one for a reading so that others can see exactly which version you used.

Contexts stay on this device until you export them. Exporting creates a file; it does not publish or release anything. Starter examples are newly written for this form. They are not endorsed by Internet Archive or promoted for Garrison Node production use.

Definition byte budget

Optionally limit each definition to a number of UTF-8 bytes. A definition over the budget is never shortened: it cannot be saved or chosen for a new reading until someone shortens the wording or changes the budget.

Measure a BitNet token budget in a separate tab · byte storage and model token capacity are separate limits.

Technical details for interested readers and developers
Internally, the portable evidence record is called a cairn. It preserves source context, readings, review decisions, and related records. Names and reviewer roles are self-declared in this browser-local prototype. Shared contribution queues and authenticated reviewers are future work.
A reading context corresponds to a Garrison Node microtheory (Mt). Its portable definition is a readable CycL subset. The current format, reckoner.context.cycl.v0.3, follows the native six-section order: a header with schema, provenance and filing facets; identity and inheritance with 5W1H emphasis; active concepts; rules; disambiguation hints; and doctrine references. Earlier versions keep their own format, v0.1 or v0.2. A version is identified by its ID, version number, and the SHA-256 of its exact UTF-8 bytes. Lists, facets and indexes are projections of that text. Compatibility with the native Garrison Node parser has not been verified here; it is tested separately on the owner’s machine. Open a context under Contexts to read its definition text.
